questions.stem: Revenue and expense accounts are closed at the end of each reporting period so that the next period starts from zero. Which accounting assumption does this apply?
questions.explanation: The period assumption divides the life of the business into reporting periods, so revenue and expenses must be measured separately for each one, which is why they are closed off. Going concern assumes the business continues; it does not explain why profit is measured period by period.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale reports its shop fittings at cost less accumulated depreciation rather than at the price they would fetch if sold today. Which assumption supports this?
options: the entity assumption, as the fittings belong to the business
the accrual basis assumption, as the fittings were bought on credit
the going concern assumption, as the business will keep using the fittings
the period assumption, as the fittings are used over several periods
questions.explanation: Because the business is assumed to continue operating, its assets are reported at the value of their continuing use rather than at what they would raise in a sale. If the business were about to close, what the assets would sell for would become relevant.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale presents its Income Statement in the same format and with the same expense classifications each year. Which qualitative characteristic does this most directly support?
questions.explanation: Using consistent formats and classifications lets the owner identify similarities and differences between periods, which is comparability. Verifiability depends on keeping source documents, not on how the report is laid out.

questions.stem: Which document would give Wattle Wholesale independent evidence of all EFT receipts and payments through its account for the month?
questions.explanation: The bank statement is prepared by the bank and lists every deposit and withdrawal, so it provides independent evidence of the business's EFT receipts and payments. A statement of account comes from a supplier and covers only that supplier's dealings.

questions.stem: The Bank account of Wattle Wholesale has debit entries totalling $48,000 and credit entries totalling $41,500 for the month. How is the account balanced?
options: Balance c/d $6,500 on the credit side; closed to the Profit and Loss Summary
Balance c/d $89,500 on the credit side; Balance b/d $89,500 on the debit side
Balance c/d $6,500 on the credit side; Balance b/d $6,500 on the debit side
Balance c/d $6,500 on the debit side; Balance b/d $6,500 on the credit side
questions.explanation: The smaller credit side needs $6,500 to equal the debit side, so the balance carried down is entered there, and it reappears as a debit balance brought down at the start of the next period. Bank is an asset, so it is balanced and carried forward, never closed to the Profit and Loss Summary.

questions.stem: Which General Ledger account is balanced and carried forward to the next period rather than closed?
questions.explanation: Asset, liability and owner's equity accounts are balanced and carried forward, so Accounts Payable continues into the next period. Wages, Sales Returns and Discount Revenue are expense and revenue accounts, which are closed to the Profit and Loss Summary.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale's revenue accounts at year end: Sales $250,000; Sales Returns $10,000; Discount Revenue $2,000; Inventory Gain $500. What is credited to the Profit and Loss Summary in the closing entry for revenues?
questions.explanation: The study design closes all revenues, including Sales Returns, in one entry, so the credit to the Profit and Loss Summary is the net amount: $250,000 + $2,000 + $500 − $10,000 = $242,500. Ignoring the returns gives $252,500, and adding them gives $262,500.

questions.stem: In the single closing entry for revenues, the Sales Returns account is:
options: debited, because it is closed in the same way as Sales
left open, because it is transferred later to Capital
closed in a separate entry to Cost of Goods Sold
credited, because it has a debit balance that must be cleared
questions.explanation: Sales Returns has a debit balance, so it is cleared with a credit within the same entry that debits Sales and the other revenues. It is not transferred to Capital or Cost of Goods Sold; only the net amount reaches the Profit and Loss Summary.

questions.stem: After closing entries, the Profit and Loss Summary of Wattle Wholesale shows credits of $242,500 and debits of $180,000. Which entry completes the account?
options: Dr Profit and Loss Summary 62,500; Cr Capital 62,500
Dr Capital 62,500; Cr Profit and Loss Summary 62,500
Dr Profit and Loss Summary 62,500; Cr Drawings 62,500
Dr Profit and Loss Summary 62,500; Cr Bank 62,500
questions.explanation: Revenue exceeds expenses by $62,500, a net profit, which is transferred to the owner's Capital account by debiting the summary and crediting Capital. A loss would be the reverse, debiting Capital; the profit is not paid out in cash, so Bank is not involved.

questions.stem: Which entry transfers Drawings at the end of the reporting period?
options: Dr Profit and Loss Summary; Cr Drawings
Dr Drawings; Cr Profit and Loss Summary
questions.explanation: Drawings reduce the owner's equity, so their debit balance is transferred to Capital by debiting Capital and crediting Drawings. Drawings are not an expense, so they never pass through the Profit and Loss Summary.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale's owner had opening capital of $80,000, contributed a further $10,000 during the year, and took drawings of $40,000. Net profit was $62,500. What is closing capital?
questions.explanation: Closing capital is $80,000 + $10,000 + $62,500 − $40,000 = $112,500. Leaving out the contribution gives $102,500, and ignoring the drawings gives $152,500.

questions.stem: In a classified Income Statement for a trading business, net sales is calculated as:
options: Sales less Cost of Goods Sold
questions.explanation: Net sales is sales revenue after deducting sales returns, and gross profit is then found by deducting cost of sales. Sales is already recorded excluding GST, so GST is not deducted again.

questions.stem: In a classified Income Statement, where is the wages of the shop's sales assistants reported?
questions.explanation: Wages of staff who sell the goods are a cost of selling, so they belong with selling and distribution expenses. Office staff wages would be administrative, and wages are a period cost, so they are not part of cost of sales.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale had sales of $300,000, sales returns of $12,000 and cost of goods sold of $172,800. What is its gross profit margin?
questions.explanation: Net sales are $288,000 and gross profit is $288,000 − $172,800 = $115,200, so the margin is $115,200 ÷ $288,000 × 100 = 40%. Dividing by sales before returns gives 38.4%, and 60% is cost of goods sold as a share of net sales.

questions.stem: Net profit was $28,800 on net sales of $288,000. What is the net profit margin?
questions.explanation: Net profit margin is net profit ÷ net sales × 100 = $28,800 ÷ $288,000 × 100 = 10%, meaning ten cents of every sales dollar remains as profit. The figure of 90% is the share of net sales consumed by expenses, not the profit kept.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale's gross profit margin stayed at 40% for two years, but its net profit margin fell from 12% to 8%. What is the most likely cause?
options: The business reduced its selling prices to attract customers.
The business raised its selling prices on all products.
Expenses other than cost of sales grew faster than net sales.
The business paid more for its inventory from suppliers.
questions.explanation: A steady gross profit margin means the relationship between selling prices, cost of sales and net sales has not changed, so the fall in net profit margin must come from other expenses such as wages or rent. Higher purchase costs, lower selling prices or higher selling prices would all have changed the gross profit margin.

questions.stem: In the Balance Sheet, the Allowance for Doubtful Debts and Accumulated Depreciation are both:
options: deducted from the asset they relate to
questions.explanation: Both are negative asset accounts: the allowance reduces Accounts Receivable and accumulated depreciation reduces the non-current asset to its carrying value. Neither is an obligation to anyone, so neither is a liability.

questions.stem: Which item belongs in the owner's equity section of a classified Balance Sheet?
options: the loan from the owner's bank
questions.explanation: The owner's equity section shows opening capital, plus any contributions and net profit, less drawings, giving closing capital. Accounts payable, GST owed and a bank loan are all liabilities owed to outside parties.

questions.stem: A bank overdraft of $4,000 at the end of the reporting period is reported as:
questions.explanation: An overdraft means the business owes the bank money that is repayable on demand, so it is a current liability. It would only be a current asset if the bank account held a positive balance.

questions.stem: In the Cash Flow Statement, the purchase of new shop fittings for cash is classified as:
questions.explanation: Investing activities are the purchase and sale of non-current assets, such as shop fittings. Financing activities involve the owner's capital and borrowing, such as contributions, drawings and loans.

questions.stem: Which cash flow is classified as a financing activity?
options: cash paid to suppliers for inventory
cash received from the sale of an old vehicle
cash paid for wages of sales staff
questions.explanation: Financing activities change the business's capital and borrowings, so cash taken by the owner is a financing outflow. Paying suppliers and wages are operating activities, and selling a vehicle is investing.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale opened the year with $12,000 in the bank. Its net cash flows were: operating +$40,000; investing −$25,000; financing −$20,000. What is the closing bank balance?
questions.explanation: Net cash flow is $40,000 − $25,000 − $20,000 = −$5,000, and $12,000 − $5,000 = $7,000. The figure of −$5,000 is the change in cash for the year, not the closing balance.

questions.stem: Which transaction is reported in the Cash Flow Statement but NOT in the Income Statement?
options: payment of $2,000 interest on the loan
questions.explanation: Repaying loan principal reduces both cash and a liability, but it is not an expense, so it appears only as a financing outflow. Interest, wages and commission revenue are cash flows that are also an expense or a revenue, so they appear in both reports.

questions.stem: Which transaction is reported in the Income Statement but NOT in the Cash Flow Statement?
options: cash sale of inventory, $3,300 including GST
cash purchase of shop fittings, $3,300 including GST
questions.explanation: Depreciation is an expense that reduces profit but involves no movement of cash in the period. The cash sale appears in both reports, while the cash purchase of fittings and the drawings affect cash but not profit.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale earned a net profit of $50,000, yet its bank balance fell by $8,000 over the year. Which combination could explain this?
options: Credit purchases of inventory rose and suppliers were paid much more slowly.
Customers paid their accounts faster and inventory was sold more quickly.
The owner took large cash drawings and the business bought a vehicle for cash.
Depreciation expense was high and a large inventory write-down was recorded.
questions.explanation: Drawings and the purchase of a non-current asset use cash without being expenses, so cash can fall while profit is high. Depreciation and write-downs reduce profit without using cash, which works in the opposite direction, and slower payment of suppliers would leave more cash in the bank.

questions.stem: A credit sale of inventory for $5,500 including GST, with a cost of $3,000, affects the reports in the period of sale by:
options: increasing cash inflows by $5,500, with no effect on net profit
increasing net profit by $2,000, with no effect on the Cash Flow Statement
increasing net profit by $2,500 and cash inflows by $5,500
increasing net profit by $5,000, with no effect on the Cash Flow Statement
questions.explanation: Sales of $5,000 less cost of goods sold of $3,000 increases profit by $2,000 when the goods are sold, under the accrual basis. No cash is received until the customer pays, so nothing appears in the Cash Flow Statement in that period.

questions.stem: Why can a profitable trading business still run short of cash?
options: Profit is earned when sales are made, but cash arrives only when customers pay.
Profit includes the GST collected, which must be paid to the Australian Taxation Office.
Cash includes non-cash expenses such as depreciation that do not affect profit.
Profit is calculated only from cash sales, so credit sales are ignored entirely.
questions.explanation: Under the accrual basis revenue is recognised when it is earned, so credit sales, prepayments and inventory purchases can all leave cash well behind profit. Profit excludes GST altogether, and depreciation affects profit, not cash.

questions.stem: The owner of Wattle Wholesale withdraws $2,000 cash for private use. Which reports are affected?
options: the Income Statement, Balance Sheet and Cash Flow Statement
the Cash Flow Statement and the Balance Sheet only
the Income Statement and the Balance Sheet only
the Income Statement and the Cash Flow Statement only
questions.explanation: Cash drawings are a financing outflow in the Cash Flow Statement and reduce both Bank and owner's equity in the Balance Sheet. They are not an expense, so the Income Statement is unaffected.

questions.stem: A credit customer returns goods sold for $1,100 including GST; the goods cost $600. What is the effect on net profit?
questions.explanation: Sales Returns of $1,000 reduce net sales, but cost of goods sold also falls by $600 as the goods go back into inventory, so profit falls by $400. Counting only the return of $1,000 ignores the reversal of the cost of goods sold.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale earned a net profit of $30,000. Total assets were $180,000 at the start of the year and $220,000 at the end. What is the return on assets?
questions.explanation: Return on assets uses average total assets: ($180,000 + $220,000) ÷ 2 = $200,000, and $30,000 ÷ $200,000 × 100 = 15%. Using closing assets alone gives 13.6% and opening assets alone gives 16.7%.

questions.stem: Net sales were $500,000 and average total assets were $200,000. What is the asset turnover?
questions.explanation: Asset turnover is net sales ÷ average total assets, so $500,000 ÷ $200,000 = 2.5 times, meaning each dollar of assets generated $2.50 of sales. Inverting the formula gives 0.4.

questions.stem: Net profit was $25,000. The owner's capital was $90,000 at the start of the year and $110,000 at the end. What is the return on owner's investment?
questions.explanation: Return on owner's investment is net profit ÷ average capital × 100, and average capital is $100,000, so the return is 25%. Using closing capital gives 22.7%, and using opening capital gives 27.8%.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale has current assets of $84,000, including inventory of $36,000 and prepayments of $3,000. Current liabilities are $60,000. What is the quick assets ratio?
questions.explanation: Quick assets exclude inventory and prepayments: $84,000 − $39,000 = $45,000, and $45,000 ÷ $60,000 = 0.75:1. Deducting only inventory gives 0.8:1, and 1.4:1 is the working capital ratio.

questions.stem: Total liabilities are $90,000 and total assets are $225,000. What is the debt ratio, and what does it measure?
questions.explanation: The debt ratio is total liabilities ÷ total assets × 100 = 40%, showing how much of the business's assets are financed by borrowing, which is a measure of stability. Liquidity indicators such as the working capital ratio look only at the short term.

questions.stem: Net cash flow from operating activities was $45,000. Current liabilities were $28,000 at the start of the year and $32,000 at the end. What is the cash flow cover?
questions.explanation: Cash flow cover is net cash flow from operating activities ÷ average current liabilities: $45,000 ÷ $30,000 = 1.5 times. Using closing liabilities gives about 1.4 times, and inverting the formula gives 0.67.

questions.stem: Wattle Wholesale's working capital ratio is 0.9:1. Which strategy would most directly improve its liquidity?
options: buying more inventory on credit to prepare for a sale
converting part of the bank overdraft into a long-term loan
using cash to buy a new delivery vehicle outright
taking larger cash drawings to reduce the owner's capital
questions.explanation: Moving debt from an overdraft repayable on demand to a non-current loan reduces current liabilities, so the ratio rises. Buying a vehicle with cash or taking drawings reduces current assets and worsens liquidity.

questions.stem: Which strategy would most directly improve Wattle Wholesale's gross profit margin?
options: reducing the wages paid to office staff
refinancing the loan at a lower interest rate
offering larger settlement discounts to customers
negotiating lower purchase prices with suppliers
questions.explanation: Gross profit margin depends on selling prices and cost of sales, so cheaper inventory raises it directly. Office wages, interest and discounts expense are other expenses, which affect net profit margin but not gross profit.

questions.stem: Which graph is most suitable for showing the trend in a business's net profit margin over five years?
options: a scatter plot of two variables
questions.explanation: A line graph shows how one measure changes over time, so the trend in net profit margin is easy to see. A pie chart shows the parts of a single whole at one time and cannot show a trend.

questions.stem: In a report to a bank, the owner of Wattle Wholesale shows sales in a column graph whose vertical axis starts at $480,000, so a rise from $490,000 to $500,000 looks like a doubling. What is the main problem?
options: The graph is not verifiable, because graphs cannot be audited at all.
The graph breaches the entity assumption, because the bank is a separate entity.
The graph exaggerates the change and so misleads the user of the report.
The graph cannot show sales, which must be reported in a pie chart.
questions.explanation: Truncating the axis makes a 2% rise look dramatic, which presents the information in a biased way and is an ethical failing in reporting to a lender. The figures themselves may be accurate; the problem is the misleading presentation.

questions.stem: In the last week of June the owner asks the bookkeeper to record July's credit sales early so that this year's profit looks higher. What does this breach?
options: the entity assumption, as the customers are separate from the business
nothing, because the sales will be made to the same customers anyway
the accrual basis and period assumptions, as revenue is reported before it is earned
the going concern assumption, as the business may not survive until July
questions.explanation: Revenue must be recognised in the period in which it is earned, so recording July's sales in June overstates this year's profit and understates next year's, misleading anyone who relies on the reports. Whether the customers are the same is irrelevant to when revenue is earned.
